title: Modern Physics: Relativity and the Quantum
description: Special relativity, light as photons, atomic spectra, quantum behaviour and nuclear energy, each taught from the measurements that forced the idea.
audience: A capable adult who has finished Discere's two classical physics courses and is comfortable with powers, square roots and a calculator with ln. No calculus is needed. Calculations are a real part of the course, and every lesson also asks for a judgement about a real measurement.
outcomes: You'll be able to find how much a moving clock lags and how much a moving rod shortens, and say when the effect is too small to matter.
You'll be able to say which of two distant events happens first for observers in relative motion.
You'll be able to convert between mass and energy and judge whether a mass change could be seen.
You'll be able to predict what a photoelectric experiment shows and work out photon energies and photon counts.
You'll be able to compute hydrogen's spectral lines and say where the Bohr model stops working.
You'll be able to predict a double-slit pattern, estimate a momentum spread from the uncertainty principle and compare tunnelling in different barriers.
You'll be able to date a sample from its half-life and compare the energy of fission and fusion from mass defect.
You'll be able to decide whether a case needs classical, relativistic or quantum physics.

lessons.title: Time dilation
lessons.objective: Use the Lorentz factor to find how much a moving clock lags, and judge from real measurements when the effect is large enough to matter.

concepts.title: Lorentz factor
concepts.summary: The factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) by which a moving clock's tick is stretched, as measured by an observer who sees it move at speed v.

concepts.title: Proper time
concepts.summary: The time between two events as shown by a clock present at both, which every inertial observer agrees on and which is the shortest time between those events.

misconceptions: Only light-based clocks slow down, so a mechanical watch, an atomic clock or a body is unaffected. The light clock is a teaching device; every clock agreed at rest agrees when moving, and atomic clocks flown on aircraft showed the effect.

Time dilation is something you see by looking at the moving clock. What you see also includes the delay of light and a Doppler change, so the effect is established by comparing readings from synchronised clocks.
A gap of 0.08% between prediction and data means the theory has failed. The gap has to be compared with the quoted uncertainty, and here it is inside it.
sequence: Start from the light clock: a pulse bouncing between two mirrors. When the clock moves, the pulse travels a longer slanted path at the same speed c, so each tick takes longer. The Pythagorean step gives the time between ticks as gamma times the rest time.
Give gamma a few values by hand (0.1 c, 0.6 c, 0.8 c, 0.98 c) so the learner sees it stay near 1 at everyday speeds and climb steeply near c.

Real data one: cosmic-ray muons at 98% of c last about five times longer than the 2.197 microseconds of a muon at rest. The CERN storage-ring result (gamma 29.327, lifetime 64.378 microseconds) is kept for the questions and is not worked in the lesson.

Real data three: after 6 months on the ISS an astronaut is about 5 milliseconds behind. Use the expansion gamma - 1 = (1/2)(v/c)^2 to reproduce it and to say where the effect crosses 0.5% (about 0.1 c).
Close on what the effect is not: dilation applies to every clock, and it is a relation between readings compared by observers, not something seen directly.
examples: A muon at rest lasts 2.197 microseconds. At 0.98 c, gamma = 5.025, so in the ground frame it lasts 5.025 x 2.197 = 11.04 microseconds and covers 0.98 x 299,792,458 x 11.04e-6 = 3.24 km. Without dilation it would cover 0.645 km.
ISS: v = 7,700 m/s, v/c = 2.568e-5, (1/2)(v/c)^2 = 3.30e-10. Six months is about 1.58e7 s, so the lag is 3.30e-10 x 1.58e7 = 5.2 ms.

figures.shows: A light clock at rest and the same clock moving, with the slanted light path drawn in the second view and the Pythagorean triangle labelled L, v t/2 and c t/2.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the rest view and the moving view and drag the speed to see the triangle lengthen.

figures.shows: Gamma against v/c from 0 to 0.98, with marked points at 0.1, 0.6, 0.8 and 0.98.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a point along the curve to read gamma; a second readout shows the dilated tick for a 1 second rest tick.

questionPlan.sample: Muons live 2.197 microseconds at rest. A muon made in an accelerator moves at 0.995 c in the laboratory. How long does it last as measured in the laboratory, in microseconds?

Muons stored in a ring at CERN have gamma = 29.327. At rest they last 2.197 microseconds, and in the ring the measured lifetime was 64.378 microseconds. Time dilation predicts 64.43 microseconds. What does the comparison show?
questionPlan.answer: They agree to 0.8 parts per thousand, within the stated accuracy, so the data support time dilation
choices: They agree to 0.8 parts per thousand, within the stated accuracy, so the data support time dilation
The 0.05 microsecond gap shows that time dilation holds only roughly, not exactly
The lengthening comes from the ring's magnetic field and not from the muons' speed
wrongOptionNotes: RIGHT
Treats any gap as failure and ignores the quoted uncertainty.
Credits the apparatus for a lengthening that tracks speed (the same 5x at 98% of c in cosmic rays, with no ring involved).

questionPlan.sample: After 6 months on the ISS, orbiting at 7,700 m/s, an astronaut has aged about 5 milliseconds less than a person on Earth. A reader says this only applies to light clocks, so the astronaut's wristwatch and body would keep Earth time. Which reply fits the evidence?
questionPlan.answer: Atomic clocks on aircraft showed it too, and clocks that agree at rest agree in motion, so all slow
choices: The watch could differ from a light clock, but a body cannot, so only the body slows
Only light clocks slow, since the derivation uses light, so the 5 ms is an instrument effect
Atomic clocks on aircraft showed it too, and clocks that agree at rest agree in motion, so all slow
wrongOptionNotes: Splits the clocks arbitrarily; nothing in the argument separates a watch from a body.
Mistakes the teaching device for the physics; the Hafele-Keating clocks were atomic.
RIGHT

questionPlan.sample: A clock ticks 0.5% slow, meaning gamma = 1.005. What fraction of the speed of light is it moving at, to two decimal places?

historyNotes: Larmor (1897) wrote the factor for orbiting electrons and Cohn (1904) tied it to the rate of clocks; Einstein (1905) showed it concerns time itself and was first to note its reciprocity; Minkowski (1907) introduced proper time. Rossi and Hall compared cosmic-ray muons on a mountain and at sea level in 1941. Hafele and Keating flew caesium clocks in 1971.

lessons.title: Relativity of simultaneity
lessons.objective: Say which of two separated events comes first for observers in relative motion, find the size of the gap, and explain why each observer can say the other's clock runs slow.

concepts.title: Relativity of simultaneity
concepts.summary: Two events at different places that are simultaneous in one inertial frame are generally not simultaneous in another, unless the motion is perpendicular to the line joining them.

concepts.title: Reciprocity
concepts.summary: Each of two observers in relative motion measures the other's clock to run slow, with no contradiction, because each compares the other's clock with several of their own.

misconceptions: The disagreement comes from light taking different times to reach the observers. The times are assigned after allowing for light travel, using Einstein's synchronisation, and the disagreement remains.

If each observer measures the other's clock slow, one of them must be wrong. Each measures the other as the one in motion, which is no more contradictory than two people at a distance who each see the other as smaller.
The twin paradox shows that both twins should be the same age on reunion. The situation is not symmetric: the travelling twin changes inertial frames to turn round.
sequence: How a distant clock is set: send a signal, reflect it, and set the far clock to the midpoint time. This procedure assumes light has the same speed in all directions, so it is a convention that observers in motion apply to their own clocks.

Einstein's train: the platform observer measures two lightning strikes at the ends of the train as simultaneous. The observer at the middle of the train, moving forward, measures the front strike as earlier.

The same result from a flash at the centre of the carriage: the train observer says it reaches both ends together; the platform observer says the rear moves up to meet it and the front moves away, so the rear is hit first.
Quantify with the time part of the Lorentz transformation: t' = (t - vx/c^2)/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). Simultaneous events (same t) at different x get different t'.
Reciprocity and the twin: why symmetric measurements do not produce a contradiction and what breaks the symmetry.
examples: Two strikes are simultaneous on the platform and 150 m apart along the track. A train passes at 0.6 c. In the train frame they are separated by gamma v dx / c^2 = 1.25 x 0.6 x 150 / 299,792,458 = 3.75e-7 s, or 375 ns, with the front strike first.
Two flashes at the same instant, side by side across the track (perpendicular to the motion): the train observers also find them simultaneous.

figures.shows: Two views of the same carriage and flash: the platform view with the carriage moving and the train view with the platform moving, each with the light front drawn at three times.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and step the flash forward in time to see which end is reached first in each.

figures.shows: Two lightning strikes labelled front and back, with a toggle for 'platform frame' and 'train frame'.
figures.learnerAction: Place the two strikes in time order for each frame.

questionPlan.sample: On the platform, two lightning bolts hit the front and the back of a passing train at the same instant. A passenger sits at the middle of the train, which is moving forward. By the passenger's own measurements, which bolt struck first?
questionPlan.answer: The one at the front, because events ahead of the train's motion happen earlier in the train's frame
choices: Both at the same instant, since a bolt at a given place and time is the same event for everyone
The one at the front, because events ahead of the train's motion happen earlier in the train's frame
The one at the back, because the train is moving away from that bolt as it travels
wrongOptionNotes: Treats simultaneity as absolute; only events at the same place are agreed.
RIGHT
Reverses the direction of the rule by reasoning from retreat.

questionPlan.sample: Two lightning strikes are simultaneous in the platform frame and 90 m apart along the track. A train passes at 0.8 c. In the train's frame, how many nanoseconds separate the strikes?
Sort each quantity by whether every inertial observer agrees on it or it depends on the observer's frame.
questionPlan.answer: Same for every observer: The speed of light in vacuum, A clock's own reading between two events it is present at, The rest mass of a particle; Depends on the frame: Whether two distant flashes were simultaneous, The length of a rod moving past at 0.8 c, How slowly a passing clock appears to tick

items.label: The speed of light in vacuum
Whether two distant flashes were simultaneous

The length of a rod moving past at 0.8 c
The rest mass of a particle
How slowly a passing clock appears to tick

questionPlan.sample: Two observers in relative motion each measure the other's clock to run slow. One twin then flies out and back, and is younger on return. Why is there no contradiction?
questionPlan.answer: The situation is not symmetric: the traveller changes inertial frames to turn round, the other twin does not
choices: The situation is not symmetric: the traveller changes inertial frames to turn round, the other twin does not
Time dilation reverses on the way back, so the clocks would agree and the age gap is a measuring error
Only the moving clock really slows; the other observer's measurement is an optical illusion of the motion
wrongOptionNotes: RIGHT
Invents a reversal that the formula does not contain.
Denies reciprocity, which the theory requires for relative motion in a single frame.

historyNotes: Poincaré raised the idea of relative simultaneity in 1900. Lorentz used 'local time' in 1892 and 1895 without a physical reading. Einstein derived the full time transformation in 1905 from the constancy of light speed and the principle of relativity. Minkowski introduced the world line in 1908.

lessons.title: Length contraction
lessons.objective: Find the length of a moving object along its line of motion, and change frames to explain one event in two ways that agree.

concepts.title: Proper length
concepts.summary: The length of an object in its own rest frame, which is the greatest length any observer will measure for it.

concepts.title: Length contraction
concepts.summary: An object measured moving along its length is shorter by the factor 1/gamma, L = L0 / gamma, and unchanged across its width.

misconceptions: A photograph of a fast object shows it squashed. Contraction is a statement about simultaneous positions of the ends; a camera records light that left different points at different times, and a passing sphere is photographed as a rotated circle.
The rod really shortens for everyone, including its own crew. Nobody in the rod's own frame measures any change.
Contraction is an effect of speed through space on one side only. It is symmetric: each frame measures the other's rods as shorter.
Everything shrinks in every direction. Only the direction of motion is affected.
sequence: Measuring a moving length needs the two ends to be marked at the same time in the observer's frame, so the result depends on the relativity of simultaneity.
The formula L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) and a short table: 99.9% at 0.0447 c and 99% at 0.141 c, so everyday speeds give nothing measurable.
Symmetry: observers in each frame find the other's rods contracted.
The muon in two frames: in the ground frame the muon lives longer (lesson 1); in the muon's frame the atmosphere is thinner, so the trip is short enough.
Where the idea shows up: the magnetic force between parallel wires seen as contraction in the electrons' frame; why paradoxes such as the ladder resolve through simultaneity.
examples: A 100 m ship at rest, passing at 0.8 c: L = 100 / 1.667 = 60 m.

Hypothetical atmosphere layer 3.0 km thick (ground frame), muon at 0.98 c. Ground frame: dilated lifetime 11.04 microseconds gives 3.24 km, enough. Muon frame: layer is 3.0 / 5.025 = 0.597 km, crossed in 0.597 km / (0.98 c) = 2.03 microseconds, less than the 2.197 microsecond rest lifetime. Both frames say the muon arrives.

figures.shows: Speed as a fraction of c against 1/gamma for 0.0447, 0.141, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.98 and 0.995.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a speed and read the contracted length for a rod of chosen proper length.

figures.shows: The same muon trip drawn twice: ground frame (long layer, dilated clock) and muon frame (short layer, ordinary clock).
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the frame and read the distance and the time on the two labelled clocks.

questionPlan.sample: A ship is 100 m long at rest. Measured from a station it passes at 0.8 c. What length does the station measure, in metres?
Muons are made at 0.99 c at the top of a layer of air that is 4.0 km thick in the ground frame (a made-up thickness). In the muon's own frame, how long does the layer take to pass, in microseconds?
A student photographs a sphere passing at 0.9 c with a very short exposure and expects an ellipse flattened along the direction of motion. What will the photograph show?
questionPlan.answer: A circular outline that looks rotated: the camera records light that left different parts at different times
choices: A flattened ellipse, because the sphere is contracted along its direction of motion
A circular outline that looks rotated: the camera records light that left different parts at different times
An unchanged circle, since fast-moving objects look the same as stationary ones in photographs
wrongOptionNotes: Equates a measurement of simultaneous end positions with a picture.
RIGHT
Denies any visual effect; the rotation is real, it just is not the contraction.

questionPlan.sample: Observer S' moves past a rod at rest in frame S and measures it as 0.8 of its rest length. A second rod of the same rest length lies at rest in S'. What does an observer in S measure for it?
questionPlan.answer: 0.8 of its rest length, because the effect is symmetric
choices: 0.8 of its rest length, because the effect is symmetric
1.25 times its rest length, to balance the first result
Its full rest length, because only one frame can see contraction
wrongOptionNotes: RIGHT
Assumes a compensating lengthening that the formula does not contain.
Treats one frame as privileged.

historyNotes: FitzGerald (1889) and Lorentz (1892) proposed the contraction to explain the Michelson-Morley null result; Einstein (1905) removed the ad hoc character. Einstein answered Varićak in 1911 that contraction does not exist for a comoving observer but can be shown by physical means by a non-comoving one. Terrell and Penrose (1959) showed that moving objects are not photographed as contracted.

lessons.title: Mass and energy
lessons.objective: Convert between a released energy and the mass a system loses, and judge whether a given mass change is large, small, or hidden in a closed system.

concepts.title: Rest energy
concepts.summary: A body at rest has energy E = m c^2, and any change in its energy changes its mass by that energy divided by c^2.

concepts.title: Closed and open systems
concepts.summary: Mass is lost only when the released energy leaves the system; in a sealed, insulated container the total mass stays the same.

misconceptions: E = mc^2 means matter vanishes into energy. The energy keeps its mass; a sealed chamber with an explosion inside weighs the same afterwards.
Only nuclear reactions change mass. Every energy change does: a water molecule is a little lighter than its atoms, a compressed spring a little heavier.
Fission needs relativity to work. Its energy was measured directly at about 200 MeV; E = mc^2 turns a mass difference into that energy but fission theory is non-relativistic.
Newtonian kinetic energy is wrong at any speed. It is the low-speed limit of the relativistic energy and is very good for a space probe.
sequence: State the relation for a body at rest and give the scale: 1 kg corresponds to about 9.0e16 J, 25 billion kilowatt-hours, or 21.5 megatons of TNT.
Run it the other way for a real device: a bomb that yields 21 kt of TNT has lost about a gram.
Closed versus open: dynamite in a sealed chamber on a scale. Where the heat goes decides whether the mass changes.
Small changes: warming a 1 kg standard by 1 degree Celsius, a compressed spring, a spinning ball, a water molecule forming. Sort them by sign and judge which could ever be measured.
Low-speed limit: expand the energy, keep the first two terms and recover (1/2) m v^2. Use the Parker Solar Probe to show how small the correction is.
Close on nuclear scale: fission loses about 0.1% of a uranium atom's mass, and Rutherford-era radioactive energies were a million times larger than molecular changes.
examples: 1 g of mass: E = 0.001 kg x (299,792,458 m/s)^2 = 9.0e13 J, which is 21.5 kt of TNT (1 kg is 21.5 Mt).
Parker Solar Probe at 68,600 m/s: the relativistic correction to kinetic energy is 3 v^2 / (4 c^2) = 3.9e-8, against a relative uncertainty of 2.2e-5 in the gravitational constant.

figures.shows: Energy equivalents of 1 kg, 1 g and 1.5 picograms in joules, kilowatt-hours and kilotons of TNT.
figures.learnerAction: Enter a mass and read the equivalents.

figures.shows: A balance holding a sealed chamber with a stick of dynamite, before and after, with an arrow showing the heat staying inside; a second view with the chamber open and the heat leaving.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle sealed and open and read the balance.

questionPlan.sample: A fission device loses 3.0 g of mass (a made-up value). How much energy does that correspond to, in joules?
A stick of dynamite explodes inside a sealed, insulated steel chamber that stands on a balance. How does the balance reading change from before to after?
questionPlan.answer: It does not change, because the heat and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass
choices: It falls by the energy released divided by c squared, since the dynamite gives energy up
It rises, because the hot gas and light are heavier than the solid dynamite was
It does not change, because the heat and light stay in the chamber and keep their mass
wrongOptionNotes: Counts energy as leaving a system that is closed.
Treats thermal motion as an extra mass source without removing anything.

questionPlan.sample: A mission planner works out the kinetic energy of a probe moving at 68,600 m/s with (1/2) m v^2. The relativistic correction is about 4 parts in a hundred million, and the gravitational constant is known to about 2 parts in a hundred thousand. What follows?
questionPlan.answer: The correction is far below the other uncertainties, so the Newtonian expression is adequate
choices: Any speed above a few kilometres per second requires the relativistic expression in practice
The correction is far below the other uncertainties, so the Newtonian expression is adequate
The correction accumulates over every orbit until it cannot be ignored in planning
wrongOptionNotes: Sets a threshold the sources do not give; the correction scales as v squared over c squared.
RIGHT
Invents accumulation; the correction is a fractional difference in energy, not a drift.

historyNotes: Einstein's 'Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?' appeared on 21 November 1905. The neutron's discovery in 1932 allowed single-nuclide mass differences; in 1933 the lithium-7 plus proton reaction tested the equation to +/-0.5%.

lessons.title: The photoelectric effect
lessons.objective: Predict what happens to the emitted electrons when the frequency or the intensity of the light changes, and find their maximum kinetic energy from the work function.

concepts.title: Threshold frequency and work function
concepts.summary: Each metal has a minimum frequency below which no electrons are emitted, whatever the intensity, and the energy h times that frequency is the work function W, the least energy needed to free an electron.

concepts.title: Photon
concepts.summary: Light is absorbed in packets of energy hf, and an electron takes all of one packet's energy or none of it, so K_max = hf - W.

misconceptions: Brighter light gives faster electrons. Intensity changes how many electrons leave, not how much energy each has.
Very dim light of any colour will free electrons after a wait, as the energy builds up. The delay is under a nanosecond and below threshold nothing is emitted however long you wait.
A bright enough lamp below the threshold frequency will eventually work. More low-energy photons never add up to one high-energy photon.
Both the stopping voltage and the current rise with intensity. Only the current does.
sequence: The apparatus: light on a clean metal plate in a vacuum tube, a collector, and a retarding voltage that stops the fastest electrons (the stopping potential).

Three observations a wave picture cannot give: a threshold frequency, electron energy independent of intensity, and no delay. Set the wave prediction (energy accumulates, dim light is delayed) beside each.
Einstein's 1905 proposal: light arrives in quanta of energy hf. State K_max = hf - W and V0 = (h/e)(f - f0).
Run it on a made-up metal with W = 2.3 eV at 400 nm and at 700 nm, and double the intensity of each.
Straight-line data: stopping voltage against frequency, slope h/e. Mention Millikan's 1914 test and that the idea was resisted at first.
Beyond the laboratory: the photomultiplier, spacecraft charging in sunlight, and measuring binding energy from photoelectron energies.
examples: W = 2.3 eV (made up). Threshold frequency = 2.3 / 4.1357e-15 = 5.56e14 Hz, wavelength 539 nm.
400 nm light: photon energy 1239.84 / 400 = 3.10 eV, so K_max = 3.10 - 2.30 = 0.80 eV and V0 = 0.80 V. 700 nm light: 1.77 eV, below 2.3 eV, so no electrons at any intensity.

figures.shows: K_max against light frequency for the lesson's 2.3 eV metal: a straight line with slope h and a frequency-axis intercept at the threshold. The work function is fixed, so the questions' metals are not shown.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a point along the line to read K_max at a chosen frequency.

figures.shows: Three observations as rows, with columns 'Wave picture predicts', 'Observed' and 'Photon picture says' (the last hidden until the learner commits to a prediction).
figures.learnerAction: Predict each row before revealing the photon column.

questionPlan.sample: A clean metal plate ejects electrons under dim ultraviolet light and none under a very bright red lamp. Which explanation fits the photon account?
questionPlan.answer: Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to free an electron; each red photon falls short, however many arrive
choices: Each ultraviolet photon has enough energy to free an electron; each red photon falls short, however many arrive
Ultraviolet light carries more power than red light, so it pushes harder on the electrons
A bright red lamp is still too dim at the surface, so the electrons need longer to gather enough energy
wrongOptionNotes: RIGHT
Confuses power (intensity) with energy per photon; the bright red lamp has more power.
Keeps the wave idea that energy accumulates; no emission occurs below threshold and any lag is under a nanosecond.

questionPlan.sample: A metal has a work function of 1.9 eV (a made-up value). Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, in eV?
A tube is lit with blue light and a stopping voltage is measured. The lamp's intensity is then doubled. What happens to the stopping voltage and to the photocurrent?
questionPlan.answer: The stopping voltage stays the same and the photocurrent doubles
choices: The stopping voltage doubles and the photocurrent stays the same
Both the stopping voltage and the photocurrent double
The stopping voltage stays the same and the photocurrent doubles
wrongOptionNotes: Assigns the intensity to electron energy, as the wave picture would.
Doubles the energy per electron as well as their number.
RIGHT

questionPlan.sample: Stopping voltage against frequency for a made-up metal: 4.84e14 Hz gives 0 V, 6.00e14 Hz gives 0.48 V and 7.50e14 Hz gives 1.10 V. The points lie on a straight line. The slope of that line equals which fundamental constant divided by the electron charge?
questionPlan.answer: The Planck constant (h)

historyNotes: Hertz observed the effect in 1887. Lenard found in 1902 that electron energy did not depend on intensity. Planck proposed energy packets in 1900 for black-body radiation; Einstein applied the idea to the photoelectric effect in 1905. Millikan showed in 1914 that the linear prediction was correct. Gilbert N. Lewis named the photon in a letter published in 1926.

lessons.title: Photon energy and photon counts
lessons.objective: Convert between wavelength, frequency and photon energy in electron-volts, and compare beams by photons per second as well as by power.

concepts.title: Photon energy
concepts.summary: A photon of frequency f has energy E = hf = hc / wavelength, and hc is 1239.84 eV nm.

concepts.title: Photon rate
concepts.summary: A beam's power is the number of photons per second times the energy of each, so beams of equal power carry more photons per second at longer wavelengths.

misconceptions: A brighter beam has more energetic photons. Brightness is photons per second; energy per photon depends only on frequency.
Two beams of equal power deliver equal numbers of photons. They do only at the same wavelength.
The electron-volt is a unit of voltage. It is a unit of energy, 1.602e-19 J.
The photon picture replaces the wave picture. Both are needed, each showing in different experiments.
sequence: E = hf with h in J s, then the electron-volt as the natural unit for atomic energies.
Combine with c = f times wavelength to get E = hc / wavelength, and use hc = 1239.84 eV nm for quick work.
Walk the visible spectrum: 400 nm is 3.10 eV, 550 nm is 2.25 eV, 700 nm is 1.77 eV; infrared photons carry less. Relate these to the few-eV energies that free electrons from metals.
From power to photon count: rate = P / E. Do a 1 mW beam at 550 nm and at 1000 nm.
Photons are counted one at a time by devices like the photomultiplier, and arrive one at a time even when they build a wave pattern (forward link to lesson 9).
Photons also carry momentum, shown by Compton's experiments of 1922 to 1924 and used in solar sails and laser cooling.
examples: 550 nm: E = 1239.84 / 550 = 2.254 eV = 3.61e-19 J. A 1.0 mW beam at that wavelength sends 1.0e-3 / 3.61e-19 = 2.77e15 photons per second; at 1000 nm (1.24 eV) it sends 5.03e15.
Two 5 mW beams at 400 nm and 800 nm: the 800 nm beam has photons of half the energy, so twice the photons per second.

lessons.title: Hydrogen's spectral lines
lessons.objective: Calculate the wavelengths of hydrogen's emission lines from the Rydberg formula and read a measured line as a jump between two energy levels.

concepts.title: Spectral series
concepts.summary: Hydrogen's lines fall in families named by the level they end on: Lyman on n = 1, Balmer on n = 2 and Paschen on n = 3.

concepts.title: Energy-level jump
concepts.summary: A line's photon energy is the difference between two level energies, so 1/wavelength = R(1/nf^2 - 1/ni^2), with R about 1.0974e7 per metre.

misconceptions: The photon's energy equals the energy of the level the electron lands on, or the one it leaves. It equals the difference between them.
The electron radiates continuously as it circles the nucleus. In Bohr's model it radiates only when it jumps between allowed orbits.
All of hydrogen's lines come from one pair of levels. Each line is a different jump; the series share the lower level.
Emission lines can be predicted only by fitting. Bohr's model gave the Rydberg formula and its constant from fundamental constants.
sequence: Start with measured lines before any theory: Balmer's 1885 formula and Rydberg's generalisation fitted them; Bohr was shown the formula in February 1913 and later wrote that everything became clear.
Use the Rydberg formula to compute the first Balmer lines (3 to 2, 4 to 2, 5 to 2, 6 to 2) and compare them with measured values from NIST.
Name the series and show where each lies: Balmer in the visible, Lyman in the ultraviolet, Paschen in the infrared.
Turn the formula into energies: with hcR = 13.606 eV the levels are -13.606/n^2 eV, and the photon energy is the difference. (This step is a short derivation, not stated in the pack.)
State Bohr's postulates in plain words: allowed orbits do not radiate; light is emitted or absorbed in a jump with E = hf; the lowest orbit has radius 52.9 pm.
Rydberg-Ritz: lines come from differences between terms, which Bohr read as energy levels.
examples: 3 to 2: 1/wavelength = 1.0974e7 x (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.524e6 per metre, so 656.1 nm and 1.89 eV (NIST measures 656.279 nm). 4 to 2: 486.0 nm (NIST 486.135). 5 to 2: 433.9 nm (NIST 434.047). 6 to 2: 410.1 nm (NIST 410.173).
NIST also lists 1875.13 nm; with a lower level of 3 the formula gives an upper level of 4, the first Paschen line.

historyNotes: Balmer's formula dates from 1885 and was generalised by Rydberg; Bohr published three papers in 1913. The Rydberg-Ritz combination principle related line frequencies to differences between terms, which Bohr read as energy levels divided by h.

lessons.title: Limits of the Bohr model
lessons.objective: Judge whether the Bohr model can be trusted for a given atom or spectral feature, and say how de Broglie's waves explain its quantisation rule.

concepts.title: Domain of the Bohr model
concepts.summary: It gives almost exact results where two charged points orbit at speeds far below c: hydrogen, singly ionised helium, doubly ionised lithium, positronium. It fails for neutral helium and for most other features of spectra.

concepts.title: Standing-wave quantisation
concepts.summary: De Broglie's wavelength h/mv fitted a whole number of times around the orbit, n wavelength = 2 pi r, gives m v r = n h-bar.

misconceptions: Electrons orbit the nucleus like planets. In modern quantum mechanics hydrogen's electron is a spherical cloud of probability, and the true ground state has zero orbital angular momentum.
Because the model is obsolete it is useless. It is exact enough for one-electron systems and is still the simplest way into energy-level diagrams.
The quantisation rule was arbitrary. De Broglie (1924) turned it into a standing-wave condition.
What works for hydrogen scales to heavier atoms. The model does not work for neutral helium.
sequence: The two ingredients: a circular classical orbit held by the Coulomb force, and a quantum rule that angular momentum is a whole number times h-bar. Results: orbit radius 52.9 pm for n = 1 and levels that reproduce the Rydberg formula.

Where it works: the list of one-electron systems and slow electrons. Where it fails: neutral helium and other multi-electron atoms, relative line intensities, fine structure, the Zeeman effect, close pairs of lines.
A specific wrong prediction: the model's ground state has angular momentum h-bar and experiment says zero.
The standing-wave reading: de Broglie's wavelength fitted around the orbit, with n whole wavelengths, so the rule is no longer arbitrary.
What replaced it: Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and Schrödinger's wave mechanics in 1925 and 1926, and the picture of a probability cloud.
examples: An orbit with n = 3 has three wavelengths around its circumference and angular momentum 3 h-bar. An orbit with 2.5 wavelengths would not meet itself after one turn.
A table of cases: Balmer wavelengths (works), He+ lines (works), neutral helium levels (fails), relative line brightness (fails), Zeeman splitting (fails), positronium levels (works).

figures.learnerAction: Step n up and down, including a fractional value that does not close.

lessons.title: Waves and particles
lessons.objective: Predict the pattern that electrons or photons make in a double-slit experiment, with and without detectors at the slits, and compute a de Broglie wavelength.

concepts.title: Wave-particle duality
concepts.summary: Photons and electrons show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others; one electron at a time lands at a single point, and the points build up a wave pattern.

concepts.title: De Broglie wavelength
concepts.summary: A particle of mass m and speed v has wavelength h / (m v).

misconceptions: The bands come from electrons interfering with each other. They build up even when electrons arrive one at a time.
Each electron goes through one slit, so the screen should show two stripes. The pattern is bands, and a detector at the slits removes them.
Duality means an object changes between wave and particle as it likes. What it shows depends on the experiment.
Only tiny things have waves. Everything does, but a thrown ball's wavelength is far too small to notice, and interference has been shown with atoms and large molecules.
sequence: Light: Young's 1801 interference showed waves; Planck's 1901 law and Einstein's 1905 photons showed particles. Electrons went the other way: Thomson measured them as particles in 1897 and de Broglie proposed electron waves in 1924.

The double slit with electrons: bands at high intensity. Turn the source down until electrons arrive one by one; each makes a dot, the dots look random, and the bands appear only as the dots accumulate.
Detectors at the slits: the bands disappear. The same happens with photons in an interferometer when the second beam splitter is removed.
Davisson and Germer and G. P. Thomson (1927) confirmed electron waves by diffraction.
Compute the wavelength h / (m v) for an electron and for a thrown ball, and say what the numbers mean.

lessons.title: The uncertainty principle
lessons.objective: Use the position-momentum inequality to find the least spread in speed for a confined particle, and decide whether the limit matters in a given case.

concepts.title: Uncertainty relation
concepts.summary: The spreads in position and momentum of a quantum state obey sigma_x sigma_p >= h-bar / 2, with h-bar = h / 2 pi.

concepts.title: Origin in waves
concepts.summary: A narrow wave packet needs many wavelengths added together, so a sharp position means a wide spread of momentum; this belongs to every wave and is not a limit of instruments.

misconceptions: The limit exists because measuring one quantity disturbs the other, so cleverer instruments could beat it. Heisenberg used that picture first, but the limit follows from the wave nature of the particle.
It applies only to electrons and atoms. Every object has a wave, and the limit is simply negligible at everyday scales.
A short-lived excited state still has a sharply defined energy. A state that exists only briefly cannot, and the line it emits is broad.
It says nothing can be known about a particle. It limits pairs of properties, and each can be known well alone.
sequence: Add plane waves to make a narrow packet and watch the momentum range widen; the two plots are Fourier partners.
State the inequality with h-bar, and say who proved it (Kennard in 1927; Heisenberg gave the idea).
Apply it: an electron confined to 0.20 nm, and to the size of hydrogen's ground-state orbit (52.9 pm).
Heisenberg's microscope as the historical explanation, and why it is not the modern one.
Scale: a baseball confined to a millimetre, and a 100 kg interferometer mirror watched for 2 ms where the limit does matter.
Energy and lifetime: fast-decaying states have broad lines, slow-decaying states narrow lines.
examples: Electron in 0.20 nm: delta v >= 1.0546e-34 / (2 x 9.109e-31 x 2.0e-10) = 2.9e5 m/s. In 52.9 pm: 1.1e6 m/s, about 0.4% of c.
A 0.145 kg ball (made up) located to 1 mm: delta v >= 3.6e-31 m/s. A 100 kg mirror observed for 2 ms: delta z = sqrt(2 h-bar t / m) = 6.5e-20 m, which the source gives as 6e-18 cm.

lessons.title: Quantum tunnelling
lessons.objective: Judge how the chance of tunnelling changes with barrier width, barrier height and particle mass, and recognise where it operates in devices, stars and nuclei.

concepts.title: Tunnelling
concepts.summary: A particle can cross a barrier it does not have the energy to climb, because its wave extends into and through the barrier.

concepts.title: Dependence on the barrier
concepts.summary: The probability of tunnelling falls exponentially as the barrier gets wider, higher or the particle heavier, so it is large only for light particles and very thin barriers.

misconceptions: A particle tunnels by borrowing energy or heating up and climbing over. Climbing over is thermionic emission; tunnelling goes through.
Beyond some thickness nothing tunnels and below it everything does. The probability falls smoothly and steeply.
Tunnelling lets particles cross faster than light. Experiments claiming this are disputed, and relativistic theory forbids it.
Tunnelling is a rare curiosity. It sets the minimum size of transistors, drives alpha decay and keeps the Sun shining.
sequence: A ball on a hill against a wave packet meeting a barrier: most of the packet reflects, a part passes, and the chance of finding the particle on the far side is the tunnelling probability.
What controls it: width, height and mass. Test it with pairs of cases that change one thing at a time.
The optical analogue the learner has met: frustrated total internal reflection, where a second prism brought close to the first lets light tunnel across the gap.
Devices: the scanning tunnelling microscope and its 0.001 nm accuracy; cold emission in strong fields; flash memory; unwanted leakage in transistors thinner than about 1 nm.
Nuclei and stars: Gamow, Gurney and Condon explained alpha decay in 1928, and stellar cores are too cool for fusion without tunnelling.
The speed question: what the disputed experiments claim and what the theorems say.
examples: STM: with the current held constant, the tip height is adjusted by piezoelectric rods, and the voltages applied map the surface to about 0.001 nm, or 1% of an atomic diameter.
Tunnel junctions show tunnelling when the insulating layer is about 3 nm or thinner.

figures.shows: A rectangular barrier with a wave packet approaching, then three frames: the reflected packet, the packet inside, and a small transmitted packet beyond; a second panel with the barrier made wider.

lessons.title: Radioactive decay and half-life
lessons.objective: Use a half-life to predict how much of a sample remains and to date a sample from its measured activity.

concepts.title: Half-life
concepts.summary: The time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay, fixed for each nuclide, so the number remaining is N = N0 x 2^(-t / half-life).

concepts.title: Decay without memory
concepts.summary: An atom's chance of decaying in a given time does not depend on its age, so one atom's decay time cannot be predicted while a large sample decays predictably.

misconceptions: After two half-lives everything has decayed. Each half-life halves what is left, so a quarter remains.
An atom that has survived a long time is due to decay. It has no memory, and its chance in the next half-life is the same 50%.
Decay products vanish. Each decay makes a daughter nuclide, which may itself be radioactive in a chain.
All decay is the same. Alpha, beta and gamma carry different charges and penetrate matter differently.
sequence: Radioactivity as a random process for single atoms but a predictable one for many, with activity counted in becquerels (decays per second).
Rutherford's recognition that every such element decays by one exponential formula, and the halving form N = N0 x 2^(-t/T).
The no-memory assumption and why it gives exponential decay.
Types of decay by charge and penetration, daughters, chains and branching.
Half-lives run from 8.6e-23 s to more than 2e24 years, so the same law covers nearly 54 orders of magnitude.
Radiocarbon: compare a sample's activity with that of living material and read the age off the decay law.
examples: A source falls from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 9.0 h: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three half-lives, so the half-life is 3.0 h.
Carbon-14, half-life 5700 y, 14 decays per minute per gram in living carbon. A sample at 4: t = 5700 x ln(14/4) / ln 2 = 5700 x 1.807 = 10,300 y.
Bismuth-212: 35.94% alpha to thallium-208 and 64.06% beta to polonium-212, so of 10,000 atoms about 3,594 take the first route; both daughters decay to stable lead-208.

lessons.title: Binding energy, fission and fusion
lessons.objective: Use mass defect and the shape of the binding energy curve to decide whether a nuclear change releases energy, and estimate the energy per kilogram of fuel.

concepts.title: Mass defect and binding energy
concepts.summary: A nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons, and the missing mass times c^2 is the binding energy that would be needed to take it apart.

concepts.title: Binding energy curve
concepts.summary: Binding energy per nucleon rises through the light nuclei, peaks at nickel-62 and iron, and falls slowly for heavier nuclei, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy.

misconceptions: Fusion always releases energy. Fusing nuclei heavier than iron absorbs it.
Fission and fusion destroy matter. The nucleons remain; the mass difference leaves as energy.
Nuclear energy is chemical energy made larger. A nucleus is bound by about a million times more energy per particle.
Fission needs E = mc^2 to be understood. Its energy was measured directly, and E = mc^2 only converts a mass difference into it.
sequence: Mass defect: helium-4 has about 0.8% less mass than four hydrogen atoms; that missing mass is the binding energy.

The curve in three regions: rising to about sodium, a plateau from about mass 30 to 90, a slow fall. Peak at nickel-62, then iron-58 and iron-56. The fall comes from growing proton repulsion against a short-range strong force.
Fusion below the peak, fission above it; fusing two similar nuclei heavier than iron absorbs energy.
Fission: heavy nucleus into two or three lighter ones plus neutrons, about 200 MeV per fission and about 0.1% of the mass of a uranium atom.

Fusion in the Sun: four protons become a helium nucleus (two protons turning into neutrons) in a very hot gas, with tunnelling to cross the repulsion; confining it on Earth needs strong magnetic fields.
Scale: hydrogen's 13.6 eV against the deuteron's 2.22 MeV, a ratio of about 160,000.
examples: 1.0 kg of hydrogen fusing loses about 0.8% of its mass, 0.008 kg, releasing 0.008 x 8.99e16 = 7.2e14 J. 1.0 kg of uranium fissioning loses about 0.1%, releasing 9.0e13 J, so fusion gives about 8 times more per kilogram.
Per nucleon: deuterium 1.11 MeV, tritium 2.83 MeV, helium-3 2.57 MeV, iron-56 8.79 MeV, nickel-62 8.79 MeV.

lessons.title: Choosing the right physics
lessons.objective: Decide for a given case whether classical physics is enough or whether relativity or quantum theory is needed, using the size of the correction, and say what replaced the Bohr model.

concepts.title: Size of the correction
concepts.summary: Relativity matters when v/c is not small (0.5% at one tenth of c), and quantum effects matter when the scales of position, momentum or energy approach h-bar; below that, classical physics is accurate.

concepts.title: What came after the old quantum theory
concepts.summary: In 1925 and 1926 matrix mechanics and wave mechanics replaced Bohr's orbits with probability waves, and general relativity adds a gravitational effect on clocks that works against the speed effect.

misconceptions: Relativity and quantum theory make classical physics wrong. Classical results remain accurate where the corrections are tiny, as for the Parker Solar Probe's kinetic energy.
Quantum effects belong to atoms and have no everyday consequences. Chips, flash memory, microscopes and stars depend on them.
Satellite clocks need one correction. The speed effect slows them and the gravitational effect speeds them up, and both are corrected.
A gap between measurement and prediction means the theory failed. It matters only against the stated uncertainty.
sequence: Collect the course's yardsticks: 0.5% time dilation at 0.1 c, 4 parts in a hundred million at 68,600 m/s, the Bohr model's one-electron domain, and h-bar-scale spreads.
Run six cases through them and name the physics each needs.
Gravitational time dilation as the new ingredient: the ISS astronaut's clock and the GPS clocks, where two effects of opposite sign are both corrected.
Hafele and Keating's 1971 flights as a worked test: predictions and measurements with uncertainties, compared properly.
What replaced the Bohr model, and what the pack does not cover beyond it (quantum field theory, the Standard Model).

questionPlan.sample: Pick one measurement from this course where a classical prediction failed. Say what the classical prediction was, what was observed, and what idea replaced it.
questionPlan.answer: A model answer: in the photoelectric effect, wave theory predicted that electron energy grows with intensity and that dim light is delayed; the observations showed a threshold frequency, energy independent of intensity and no delay, and photons of energy hf replaced the wave account.

historyNotes: Hafele and Keating flew caesium clocks east and west in 1971. Heisenberg's Umdeutung paper (1925), matrix mechanics with Born and Jordan, and Schrödinger's wave mechanics (1925 and 1926) replaced the Bohr model.

courseCheck: A mixed set of about fourteen items, one from each lesson, with at least half asking for a judgement about data. Compute gamma and a dilated time; order two events for a moving observer; contract a length; convert a mass loss to joules; predict a photoelectric outcome from a change in frequency or intensity; turn a wavelength into photon energy and a photon rate; compute a Balmer line; sort cases the Bohr model handles; predict a double-slit screen with and without detectors; estimate a speed spread from the uncertainty relation; rank how a barrier change affects tunnelling; apply a half-life to dating; decide whether a nuclear change releases energy and how much per kilogram; and sort cases into classical, relativistic and quantum.
platformNeeds: A two-frame relativity explorer: a carriage and platform with a flash, a speed slider, and clocks in both frames showing which end is hit first and the time gap. Fallback: the svg_figure views planned in lessons 2 and 3.

A photoelectric-tube explorer: sliders for frequency and intensity and a metal's work function, showing current, K_max and stopping voltage. Fallback: graph_plot of K_max against frequency and the observations table in lesson 5.
A hydrogen energy-level explorer: levels on an eV scale, a selectable jump with its photon energy, wavelength and spectral region. Fallback: the svg_figure ladder in lesson 7.
A particle-by-particle double-slit accumulator with a detector toggle. Fallback: the three-frame svg_figure in lesson 9.
Linked position and momentum wave-packet plots with a width slider (lesson 10). Fallback: two fixed svg_figure packets.
A radioactive-decay sampler: N atoms decaying at random against the exponential curve, with a half-life slider. Fallback: sampling_population in lesson 12.
Numeric answers need a calculator widget with ln, sqrt, exp and scientific notation; several answers are of the form 8.99e16.
unverified: Made-up scenario numbers, flagged as made up in each prompt: the 2.3 eV work function and its data points, the 3.0 km layer of air, the 150 m strike separation and 0.6 c train, the 0.145 kg ball at 40 m/s, the 1 ns and 1 microsecond excited-state lifetimes, the 800 Bq source, the 1 mW and 5 mW beams, and the 1000, 700, 600 and 500 nm lamps.
The pack gives no table of real work functions, so no real metal is named with a work function.
E_n = -13.606 / n^2 eV for hydrogen is a short derivation from the Rydberg formula and the NIST value of hcR; it is not stated in the pack.

The Wikipedia carbon-14 example gives a half-life of 5700(30) years but works with 5730 years (tau 8267 y, age 10,356 y). Lessons must use their own stated half-life: with 5700 y the answer is 10,302 y.
Wikipedia dates Planck's quantum proposal to 1900 on one page and 1901 on another. Avoid the year, or say 'around 1900'.

The pack has no figure for the energy of one fission or fusion event beyond 200 MeV for fission, no list of fission products or chain-reaction details, and no binding-energy values for helium-4 or uranium. The binding curve must be drawn from the three-region description and the seven nuclides tabulated, not from remembered data.

General relativity, quantum field theory and the Standard Model appear in the pack only in passing, so lesson 14 treats 'what came after' through the 1925 to 1926 replacement of the Bohr model and gravitational time dilation, and no further.
No GPS clock-offset figure (such as microseconds per day) is in the pack; it says only that GPS clocks are corrected for both effects.
